screens.title: What is an election and when is it triggered?
screens.narratorSegment: An election in MongoDB is the coordinated process by which replica set members vote to select a new primary when the current primary is not able to serve. It is the fundamental mechanism that supports automatic failover and keeps the cluster writable. There are three typical triggers for an election. First, an unexpected primary failure — if a primary crashes, loses network connectivity, or otherwise becomes unreachable, secondaries start a countdown and then begin election behavior after the configured timeout. Second, a manual step-down via rs. stepDown forces the current primary to resign so you can perform planned maintenance without causing chaotic restarts. Third, certain replica set reconfigurations such as adding or removing voting members can prompt an election to ensure the most appropriate primary is active. A key practical point is that only voting members participate in the election and each has one vote; therefore a majority of available votes is required to elect a primary. A common misconception is that any lagging secondary will trigger an election — in fact, lag alone does not start a vote; it only affects a candidate's chance of being selected. Reflect on your cluster topology: if you lose a primary and lack a majority of votes, your replica set becomes read-only until quorum returns. How would you ensure quorum before planned maintenance?

keyIdea.title: Election triggers
keyIdea.text: Primary failure, manual step-down, and some reconfigurations start elections; majority voting is required to make a decision.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Election Definition
Definition

An election is the vote-based process that chooses a new primary when the current primary is unavailable or steps down. Voting members each cast one vote and a majority is required to elect a new primary.

Common triggers
  • Primary failure: crash, network partition, or process stop leads to timeout and election.
  • Manual step-down: rs.stepDown used for planned maintenance to trigger a graceful election.
  • Reconfiguration: topology changes can initiate a fresh primary selection.
Misconception
Replication lag on a secondary does not automatically trigger an election; lag only reduces a candidate's favorability.
Concrete example

If the primary on localhost:27017 crashes, secondaries detect the loss after the election timeout and begin nominating candidates. A member that holds an up-to-date optime and a high priority will have a better chance to win the majority vote.

Key Takeaway
Elections maintain availability but depend on quorum. Plan your voting members to avoid losing write capability.

screens.title: How voting members elect a new primary
screens.narratorSegment: Elections follow a clear multi-step process that ensures a consistent and safe transition to a new primary. First, members detect the absence of the primary after a timeout; this detection is the trigger that allows a secondary to start an election. Second, a member that wants to be primary checks its eligibility — it must be a voting member, not have buildIndexes disabled, and have up-to-date data. Third, the candidate requests votes by sending its latest optime and other status information to peers. Each voting member evaluates the candidate against its own view of the cluster and grants or denies its vote. The election succeeds only if the candidate receives a majority of votes. Fourth, once elected, the new primary transitions to PRIMARY state and informs other members; secondaries update their internal primary pointer. A common misconception is that elections are instantaneous; in realistic networks there are multiple communication rounds and timing matters. For example, network latency or an overloaded node can delay votes and extend failover time. To practice this, observe rs. status() while you simulate a primary crash: you will see nomination messages, votes cast, and finally a new primary state. How would you reduce the time to elect in your environment without risking split-brain?

keyIdea.text: Detect primary absence → nominate eligible candidate → request votes → gain majority → transition to primary.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Voting Process
Step-by-step
  1. Detection: secondaries notice the primary is unreachable after the timeout.
  2. Nomination: an eligible secondary nominates itself as candidate.
  3. Request votes: candidate asks voting members for their vote, sharing optime and status.
  4. Voting: peers grant or deny votes based on eligibility and freshness.
  5. Promotion: if majority achieved, candidate becomes primary; cluster updates follow.
Common mistake
Assuming immediate promotion. Elections require network communication and majority; poor connectivity delays failover.
Concrete scenario

If the 27017 primary fails, a secondary with the freshest optime and a high priority will request votes. If two of three voting members grant votes, it becomes primary. If quorum cannot be reached, the set remains without primary and writes stop until majority is restored.

Pro tip
Keep an odd number of voting members and colocate reliable network links between them to reduce election latency and avoid quorum loss.

screens.title: Selection criteria: priority vs optime
screens.narratorSegment: When multiple candidates are eligible during an election, MongoDB uses configuration and state to choose the best primary. Two critical factors are priority and optime. Priority is a configured value per member that ranges from zero to a high value; higher-priority members are favored in elections. A priority of zero means the member cannot become primary at all, which is useful when you want a dedicated secondary for analytics. Optime is the timestamp of the last applied operation on a member; among candidates with comparable priority, the member with the most recent optime is preferred to minimize potential data loss. Votes and buildIndexes also matter: a member with buildIndexes set to false cannot become primary. Consider a case where a preferred high-priority node has significant replication lag; despite its priority, its stale optime may cause peers to deny its vote in favor of a fresher node. A common misconception is to only tune priorities; you must also ensure replication keeps optime reasonably current. The practical takeaway is to align priority settings with network performance and hardware so that the most likely primary is both preferred and up to date.

keyIdea.text: Priority steers preference; optime ensures the promoted primary has recent data. Tune both for predictable, safe failovers.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Priority vs Optime
Priority

Configured per member (0 to 1000). Higher values increase election preference. A priority of 0 prevents promotion, useful for dedicated secondaries.

Optime

Represents the timestamp of the last applied operation. Candidates with fresher optime are preferred to reduce possible data loss on failover.

Misconception
Higher priority always wins. In reality, a high-priority but stale node can lose to a fresher lower-priority node.
Side-by-side scenario
Node A
priority: 10
optime: t0 - 10s
Node B
priority: 5
optime: t0 - 1s
In this example Node B may be chosen because its optime is more recent despite lower priority. To avoid surprises, keep replication fast for your preferred primaries.
Key takeaway
Align priority with replication performance so preferred primaries are also up to date.

screens.title: Using rs.stepDown() for planned maintenance
screens.narratorSegment: rs. stepDown allows you to gracefully move a primary to secondary to perform maintenance while triggering a controlled election. The command takes a seconds argument that specifies how long the stepping down node should refrain from seeking primary status. A common pattern is to step down for a period long enough for a new primary to be elected, for example 60 or 300 seconds. To use it, connect to the current primary with the shell, execute rs. stepDown with a reasonable timeout, and expect the shell to disconnect as leadership changes. After the step-down completes and a new primary is elected, reconnect and verify states using rs. status(). A practical example: you are applying OS updates to the primary. Running rs. stepDown(60) forces a handover; the old primary will not immediately campaign to regain leadership, reducing oscillation. Important safety checks: ensure there are enough healthy voting members to form a majority before stepping down, otherwise you can leave the set without a writable primary. Also, be aware that application drivers should be configured with the replica set name and multiple hosts so they can discover the new primary automatically. When might you choose a longer step-down period, and why?

keyIdea.title: rs.stepDown safety
keyIdea.text: Use rs.stepDown(<seconds>) with enough healthy voting members available to guarantee a new primary can be elected during maintenance.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › rs.stepDown Walkthrough
Example commands
// Connect to the current primary
mongosh --port 27017

// Step down the primary for 60 seconds
rs.stepDown(60)
When you run rs.stepDown, the shell usually disconnects because the server is changing role. After the election completes, reconnect to any member and use rs.status() to confirm which node is now primary.
Checklist before stepDown
  • Confirm at least majority of voting members are healthy.
  • Ensure replication lag is low on preferred candidates.
  • Inform applications of expected transient disconnects.
Gotcha
If no majority exists during step-down, writes will stop until quorum is restored. Never step down into an unavailable quorum.

screens.title: Voting members and quorum design
screens.narratorSegment: Quorum — having a majority of voting members — is the backbone of reliable elections. Each voting member has one vote. For a candidate to be elected, it must collect more than half of the votes from available voting members. This is why an odd number of voting members is recommended: with three voting members, the set tolerates one failure and still elects a leader; with four, one failure could leave the set unable to find a strict majority. Arbiters are voting members that do not hold data; they can help maintain an odd number of votes without the resource cost of a full data-bearing node, but they do not help with read or write throughput. A common design mistake is relying on too few voting nodes or placing multiple voting members behind a single point of failure. Also, network partitions can split the set into two groups; only the group with majority continues to elect a primary. For robust architecture, place voting members across reliable, low-latency networks and ensure monitoring alerts when replication lag or unreachable nodes appear. Reflect: which nodes in your deployment should be voting members and which can be non-voting secondaries?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Quorum & Voting
Voting member concepts
  • One vote per voting member: majority required to elect.
  • Odd number recommended: prevents tie scenarios when a node fails.
  • Arbiters: provide votes without storing data, helpful to reach odd counts.
Pitfall
Placing multiple voting members in the same failure domain can still cause quorum loss if that domain fails.
Concrete guidance
For a small production replica set, use three data-bearing voting members across separate hosts. Add an arbiter only if you need an extra vote and cannot add a full member. Monitor health and replication performance to ensure elections succeed when needed.
Key takeaway
Design voting layout to preserve majority under realistic failure scenarios.

screens.title: Automatic failover timeline
screens.narratorSegment: Automatic failover is the observable flow between detecting primary absence and finishing a new election. Imagine the primary goes down at time zero. Secondaries run a configurable timeout (by default around 10 seconds) and then begin the election protocol. During those seconds applications might experience transient errors or reconnect attempts. A candidate nominates itself and requests votes; peers evaluate and vote based on priority, optime, and eligibility. If a majority grants votes, the candidate steps into primary state and replication resumes with the new leader. In many healthy three-member sets this completes in seconds. However, timeline length increases if nodes experience high latency, heavy load, or slow replication. A key misconception is thinking the timeout is the only delay; actual election time includes communication rounds and clock skew handling. Observe logs and rs. status() during an experiment to see the timeline on your infrastructure. Practically, keeping replication up to date and minimizing network jitter shortens failover time and reduces the window where clients must retry writes. Automatic failover timeline means failover includes detection timeout and voting rounds; optimize replication and network to shorten it.. In practical terms, from primary failure to new primary elected. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: Several operational mistakes commonly cause election and failover pain. First, misconfigured priorities — assigning high priority to a node that is resource-constrained or network-isolated — can result in repeated elections or promotion of a node that cannot handle production load. Second, having too few voting members or an even number of votes can leave your set without a majority after a single failure, making the set read-only until quorum is restored. Third, network partitions that isolate subsets of members can appear to each partition as if the primary is down; while MongoDB's majority requirement prevents both sides from becoming primary, severe partitions and misplacement of voting members can still lead to unexpected unavailability. To avoid these problems, choose an odd number of voting members, place them across healthy failure domains, and set priorities after measuring replication lag. Also, avoid overusing arbiters except when you need an extra vote and cannot add a full data-bearing member. If you face repeated elections, check replication lag, member health, and the priority map. What monitoring signals would you check first when you see multiple elections in a short window?

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Common Mistakes
Common mistakes
  • Bad priority choices: promoting underpowered or lagging nodes.
  • Too few voting members: losing quorum after one failure.
  • Network partitions: split visibility causing delayed or failed elections.
Diagnostics
Check rs.status(), replication lag, server logs, and network metrics. Repeated elections often point to connectivity or replication problems rather than election logic itself.
Action
Fix the root cause: improve connectivity, tune replication, or adjust priorities — not just restart mongod processes repeatedly.

Majority & Quorum

Priority & Freshness

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how MongoDB replica sets detect a primary problem and elect a new primary without manual intervention. Elections are the automatic vote-based process that keeps writes available by selecting the most suitable candidate among the remaining members. We'll cover the common triggers for an election — such as an unexpected primary failure, a manual step-down for maintenance, and certain reconfigurations — and the selection criteria MongoDB uses, including priority and optime. You'll also see how rs. stepDown is used intentionally to cause a graceful failover during planned work. Understanding these mechanics matters because it helps you design replica sets that fail over quickly and safely. For example, setting appropriate priorities and ensuring an odd number of voting members reduces the chance of losing a majority and keeps your cluster writable. We'll also highlight common mistakes like network partitions and misconfigured votes, which can lead to unplanned downtime or split-brain risk. After this overview you will be able to reason about failover behavior and plan maintenance with confidence.

By the end of these lesson objectives you will clearly explain when MongoDB starts an election, describe how voting members choose a new primary, identify the practical criteria used for selection, and perform a manual step-down for planned maintenance. First, you will learn the three common triggers for an election: unplanned primary failure, explicit rs. stepDown, and replica set reconfiguration. Understanding triggers lets you reason about when the cluster will attempt to promote someone else. Second, you'll be able to walk through the vote sequence: members detect primary absence, nominate candidates, and vote; a majority is required. Third, you'll connect configuration settings such as priority and optime to real outcomes so you can shape which member becomes primary in normal and degraded states. Finally, you'll practice a controlled step-down using rs. stepDown so that you can run maintenance with minimal disruption. Each objective pairs a skill with why it matters, and together they help you design, operate, and troubleshoot high-availability replica sets with predictable behavior.

We'll use a Bloom-style progression to structure your learning. First, you'll learn the facts: what triggers an election and what selection criteria exist. Next, you'll understand the reasons behind each criterion, such as why a higher priority and a recent optime make a candidate preferable. Then you'll practice applying those facts by performing a controlled rs. stepDown and observing the election outcome. Finally, you'll be able to reason about and design safe replica sets — choosing the right number of voting members and setting priorities to reduce downtime risk. Each objective builds on the previous one: factual knowledge enables understanding, which enables correct application during maintenance, which leads to mastery of designing robust clusters. This structure helps you not only follow the mechanics but also make sound operational choices in real deployments.

An election in MongoDB is the coordinated process by which replica set members vote to select a new primary when the current primary is not able to serve. It is the fundamental mechanism that supports automatic failover and keeps the cluster writable. There are three typical triggers for an election. First, an unexpected primary failure — if a primary crashes, loses network connectivity, or otherwise becomes unreachable, secondaries start a countdown and then begin election behavior after the configured timeout. Second, a manual step-down via rs. stepDown forces the current primary to resign so you can perform planned maintenance without causing chaotic restarts. Third, certain replica set reconfigurations such as adding or removing voting members can prompt an election to ensure the most appropriate primary is active. A key practical point is that only voting members participate in the election and each has one vote; therefore a majority of available votes is required to elect a primary. A common misconception is that any lagging secondary will trigger an election — in fact, lag alone does not start a vote; it only affects a candidate's chance of being selected. Reflect on your cluster topology: if you lose a primary and lack a majority of votes, your replica set becomes read-only until quorum returns. How would you ensure quorum before planned maintenance?

Elections follow a clear multi-step process that ensures a consistent and safe transition to a new primary. First, members detect the absence of the primary after a timeout; this detection is the trigger that allows a secondary to start an election. Second, a member that wants to be primary checks its eligibility — it must be a voting member, not have buildIndexes disabled, and have up-to-date data. Third, the candidate requests votes by sending its latest optime and other status information to peers. Each voting member evaluates the candidate against its own view of the cluster and grants or denies its vote. The election succeeds only if the candidate receives a majority of votes. Fourth, once elected, the new primary transitions to PRIMARY state and informs other members; secondaries update their internal primary pointer. A common misconception is that elections are instantaneous; in realistic networks there are multiple communication rounds and timing matters. For example, network latency or an overloaded node can delay votes and extend failover time. To practice this, observe rs. status() while you simulate a primary crash: you will see nomination messages, votes cast, and finally a new primary state. How would you reduce the time to elect in your environment without risking split-brain?

When multiple candidates are eligible during an election, MongoDB uses configuration and state to choose the best primary. Two critical factors are priority and optime. Priority is a configured value per member that ranges from zero to a high value; higher-priority members are favored in elections. A priority of zero means the member cannot become primary at all, which is useful when you want a dedicated secondary for analytics. Optime is the timestamp of the last applied operation on a member; among candidates with comparable priority, the member with the most recent optime is preferred to minimize potential data loss. Votes and buildIndexes also matter: a member with buildIndexes set to false cannot become primary. Consider a case where a preferred high-priority node has significant replication lag; despite its priority, its stale optime may cause peers to deny its vote in favor of a fresher node. A common misconception is to only tune priorities; you must also ensure replication keeps optime reasonably current. The practical takeaway is to align priority settings with network performance and hardware so that the most likely primary is both preferred and up to date.

rs. stepDown allows you to gracefully move a primary to secondary to perform maintenance while triggering a controlled election. The command takes a seconds argument that specifies how long the stepping down node should refrain from seeking primary status. A common pattern is to step down for a period long enough for a new primary to be elected, for example 60 or 300 seconds. To use it, connect to the current primary with the shell, execute rs. stepDown with a reasonable timeout, and expect the shell to disconnect as leadership changes. After the step-down completes and a new primary is elected, reconnect and verify states using rs. status(). A practical example: you are applying OS updates to the primary. Running rs. stepDown(60) forces a handover; the old primary will not immediately campaign to regain leadership, reducing oscillation. Important safety checks: ensure there are enough healthy voting members to form a majority before stepping down, otherwise you can leave the set without a writable primary. Also, be aware that application drivers should be configured with the replica set name and multiple hosts so they can discover the new primary automatically. When might you choose a longer step-down period, and why?

Quorum — having a majority of voting members — is the backbone of reliable elections. Each voting member has one vote. For a candidate to be elected, it must collect more than half of the votes from available voting members. This is why an odd number of voting members is recommended: with three voting members, the set tolerates one failure and still elects a leader; with four, one failure could leave the set unable to find a strict majority. Arbiters are voting members that do not hold data; they can help maintain an odd number of votes without the resource cost of a full data-bearing node, but they do not help with read or write throughput. A common design mistake is relying on too few voting nodes or placing multiple voting members behind a single point of failure. Also, network partitions can split the set into two groups; only the group with majority continues to elect a primary. For robust architecture, place voting members across reliable, low-latency networks and ensure monitoring alerts when replication lag or unreachable nodes appear. Reflect: which nodes in your deployment should be voting members and which can be non-voting secondaries?

Automatic failover is the observable flow between detecting primary absence and finishing a new election. Imagine the primary goes down at time zero. Secondaries run a configurable timeout (by default around 10 seconds) and then begin the election protocol. During those seconds applications might experience transient errors or reconnect attempts. A candidate nominates itself and requests votes; peers evaluate and vote based on priority, optime, and eligibility. If a majority grants votes, the candidate steps into primary state and replication resumes with the new leader. In many healthy three-member sets this completes in seconds. However, timeline length increases if nodes experience high latency, heavy load, or slow replication. A key misconception is thinking the timeout is the only delay; actual election time includes communication rounds and clock skew handling. Observe logs and rs. status() during an experiment to see the timeline on your infrastructure. Practically, keeping replication up to date and minimizing network jitter shortens failover time and reduces the window where clients must retry writes. Automatic failover timeline means failover includes detection timeout and voting rounds; optimize replication and network to shorten it.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

To learn by doing, perform a controlled unplanned failover on your three-member replica set. Start by connecting to any node and running rs. status() to identify the current primary. Next, stop the mongod process for that primary — for example by sending a stop signal to the terminal or stopping the service. Immediately reconnect to one of the remaining nodes and observe rs. status() repeatedly. You should see the former primary marked as down and an election sequence as secondaries nominate and vote. Once a majority votes, a new primary will be promoted; note which node becomes primary and its optime. Restart the original node and reconnect to the cluster; it should rejoin as a secondary.
